why: Anything in quotes is a string, even if it looks like a number.
With a string present, + concatenates instead of adding.
The - operator converts the string to a number first.

q: Which keyword declares a variable that cannot be reassigned?
why: const creates a binding that can't be reassigned.
Math.max returns the largest argument.

q: Which array method adds an item to the end?
why: push() appends; pop() removes the last item.
== compares after type conversion, so "5" and 5 are equal.
An empty string is falsy.
map() returns a new array with each value doubled.
A famous quirk: typeof null is "object".
Spread turns the string into characters, which are reversed and joined back.
A declared variable with no value is undefined.
filter() keeps only the items where the callback returns true.
const prevents reassignment, not changing the object's properties.
1 < 2 is true, then true < 3 becomes 1 < 3 (true). 3 > 2 is true, then true > 1 becomes 1 > 1 (false).
sort() without a comparator sorts items as strings, so "10" comes before "9".
var is function-scoped, so all callbacks share one i, which is 3 when the timers fire.
let creates a fresh binding for each loop iteration.
Binary floating-point can't represent 0.1 and 0.2 exactly.

q: What is the order of the output?
why: Synchronous code first (1, 4), then microtasks (promise → 3), then timers (2).
Both operands are converted to strings: "" + "[object Object]".
Arrow functions use the this of the surrounding method, here the object o.
NaN is the only value that is not equal to itself. Use Number.isNaN() to test.
Function declarations are hoisted above var assignments, so foo is already the function.

title: Sum of a list
statement: Return the sum of all the numbers in the list. An empty list should return 0.
hint: Start with a total of 0 and add each number to it in a loop.

title: Even or odd
statement: Return true if the number is even, otherwise false.
hint: A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is 0.

title: Reverse a string
hint: Python slices with [::-1]. In JavaScript: split into characters, reverse, join.

title: Count the vowels
statement: Return how many vowels (a, e, i, o, u — upper or lower case) are in the text.
hint: Convert to lower case first so you only check five letters.

title: Palindrome check
statement: Return true if the text reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring upper/lower case and any character that is not a letter or digit.

examples.call: isPalindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")

hint: Build a cleaned version containing only letters and digits in lower case, then compare it with its reverse.
tests: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

title: FizzBuzz
statement: Return a list of strings for 1..n: "Fizz" for multiples of 3, "Buzz" for multiples of 5, "FizzBuzz" for both, otherwise the number as a string.
hint: Check the multiple-of-15 case first, otherwise it will be caught by the Fizz or Buzz branch.

title: Two Sum
statement: Given a list of numbers and a target, return the two indexes [i, j] (with i < j) whose values add up to the target. Exactly one solution exists.
hint: Store each number's index in a dictionary/Map as you go, and look up target - current before storing.

title: Group the anagrams
statement: Group words that are anagrams of each other. Return a list of groups; sort the words inside each group alphabetically, and sort the groups by their first word.
hint: Two words are anagrams when their sorted letters are identical — use the sorted letters as a dictionary key.

title: Longest substring without repeats
statement: Return the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated character.
hint: Slide a window: remember the last index of each character, and move the window start just past a repeat.
